1.open: Who gave you a piece of advice when you were younger that you ignored at the time but later wished you had followed?
questions: Verses 2 to 4 say this book is for gaining "wisdom and discipline" and for giving "prudence to the simple." What do you think wisdom is, and how is it different from being smart?
Verse 7 says "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge." What do you think fearing the LORD means here, and why might it come first?
The writer says fools "despise wisdom and discipline" (v. 7). In this book a fool is less about low intelligence and more about refusing to be taught. When do you find it hardest to take correction?
Verses 8 and 9 name both a father and a mother as teachers. Who has taught you the most about how to live, and what did they give you that you still carry?
The gang in verses 10 to 14 promises plunder and an easy share of the take. What are the modern versions of that kind of invitation, and what makes them hard to turn down?
Verse 18 says those men "lie in wait for their own blood." How can a choice that seems to be aimed at someone else end up hurting the person who makes it?
Wisdom "calls out in the street" and in the square (vv. 20, 21). If wisdom is that public, why do so many people still miss it, and what noise drowns it out for you?

Wisdom's words in verses 24 to 32 are hard, and her laughter at ruin is a harsh picture. If you have ever felt that God is distant or silent, or that you have waited too long, what do you make of this passage, and what do you want to say about it honestly?
1.life: This week, ask one person you trust for honest advice about something you are deciding, then listen all the way through without defending yourself. Afterwards, thank them and think about what you heard.
1.prayer: Ask God for a teachable heart that can hear correction without getting defensive. Pray for the people who have taught you, and for the humility to keep learning.
1.tip: Verses 24 to 32 can sound as if God shuts the door on anyone who waited too long, and a doubting or guilty person may hear it that way. Name that fear gently. Point out that the passage is a warning meant to wake people up, and that Wisdom is still calling out in public. If someone wants to ask whether Wisdom here is just a picture of God's wisdom or points ahead to Jesus, say that Christians read it both ways and move on.

2.open: Have you ever lost something and searched for it much longer than you expected? What was it, and did you find it?
questions: The chapter opens with a string of "if" lines: accept, hide, incline, call out, seek, search (vv. 1-4). Which of these feels hardest for you right now, and why?
Verse 4 says to seek wisdom "like silver" and "search it out like hidden treasure." What is something you have searched for that hard, and what made it seem worth the effort?
Verse 6 says, "For the LORD gives wisdom." If wisdom is a gift, why does the writer also tell us to dig for it? How do those two ideas fit together?
Verse 10 says wisdom "will enter your heart, and knowledge will delight your soul." When has doing the right thing started to feel natural or even enjoyable for you, instead of a burden?
Verse 11 says "Discretion will watch over you, and understanding will guard you." Where in your life right now would you most like some good judgment standing guard?

Verses 12 to 15 describe people who "enjoy doing evil" and whose "ways are devious." How can we tell when someone's words are twisting the truth, and how do we stay kind to them while keeping our distance?

Verses 16 to 19 warn about a person who "forgets the covenant of her God." Scholars debate whether she is a real person, a picture of folly, or both. What do you take from the warning about broken promises and tempting words, whichever way it is read?
Be honest here: if you feel you have not found much wisdom yet, or you wonder whether God speaks at all, what would it take for you to keep searching?
2.life: Pick one decision you are facing this week, big or small. Before you act, set aside ten minutes to ask God for wisdom, and ask one trusted person what they think.
2.prayer: Thank God that wisdom is his gift and that he is a shield to those who walk with integrity. Ask for a hungry heart, and for good judgment in one specific place in your life.
2.tip: Verses 20 to 22 can sound like a promise that good people always stay safe and the wicked always lose. Some in the group may have seen faithful people suffer. Say plainly that Christians differ on whether these are firm guarantees or how life generally tends to go for the wise, and let people share their experience without rushing to fix it.

3.open: Who is someone whose advice you have trusted over the years, and what made you trust them?
questions: The father says to "write them on the tablet of your heart" (v. 3). What is one thing you have learned from a parent, mentor or teacher that has stayed with you?

Verse 5 says, "Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding." What does it look like to trust God in a real decision you are facing, without ignoring the brain he gave you?
Verse 7 warns, "Be not wise in your own eyes." Where do you find it hardest to take advice from others?

Verse 12 says, "the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights." How does it sit with you to hear hard times described this way? Answer honestly, even if it does not sit well.
Wisdom is called "more profitable than silver" and "better than fine gold" (v. 14). What do people around us chase that promises to be worth more than that?
Verses 2, 10 and 16 promise long life, full barns and honor. Christians differ on whether these are firm guarantees or general patterns of how life tends to go. What have you seen in real life?
Verse 24 says, "When you lie down, you will not be afraid." What tends to keep you awake at night, and what would it mean to hand that to God?
Verse 27 says, "Do not withhold good from the deserving when it is within your power to act." Where is there a good thing you could do for someone this week instead of putting it off?
3.life: Pick one decision or worry you are carrying this week. Before you act on it, pray verses 5 and 6 over it, then ask one wise person you trust for their view.
3.prayer: Thank God that he is a Father who guides and corrects out of love. Ask for a heart that trusts him more than its own cleverness, and for peace where worry keeps you awake.
3.tip: Verses 9 and 10 and the promises of long life can sound like a formula, and some in the room may have faithfully lived hard lives or buried loved ones young. Name the disagreement gently, treat Proverbs as wise sayings about how life usually goes, and let anyone share a hurt without trying to fix it.

4.open: What is one piece of advice from a parent, grandparent or mentor that stuck with you, whether you wanted it to or not?
questions: The father begins by remembering his own father's teaching, when he was "tender and the only child of my mother" (v. 3). Why might it matter that wisdom is passed down and not just announced?

Verse 7 says, "Wisdom is supreme; so acquire wisdom." The Hebrew here is a little hard to translate, but the point seems to be that wisdom starts with deciding to go after it. What would it look like for you to make that decision in a practical way?
Wisdom is pictured as someone to love and embrace, who will "guard you" and "honor you" (vv. 6, 8). How is that different from thinking of wisdom as a list of rules?

Verse 12 says, "When you walk, your steps will not be impeded; when you run, you will not stumble." Many of us have followed good advice and still stumbled. How do you read that promise in light of real life?
The way of the wicked is "like the darkest gloom; they do not know what makes them stumble" (v. 19). Have you ever stumbled over something and only later seen what was really causing it?

The path of the righteous is "like the first gleam of dawn, shining brighter and brighter until midday" (v. 18). Dawn is gradual, not instant. What does that say about growing in wisdom, especially for someone who feels stuck or unsure about faith?
Verse 23 says, "Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life." What are some things that shape your inner life each day, for better or worse?
The father moves from heart to mouth, eyes and feet (vv. 23 to 27). Which of those is hardest for you to keep steady right now, and why?
4.life: Pick one thing that feeds your inner life, like a screen habit, a conversation or a quiet moment, and change it on purpose this week. Also ask an older person what they learned the hard way, and listen.
4.prayer: Ask God for a teachable heart and for wisdom that grows like the dawn. Pray for those who have taught you, and for anyone you may be able to teach.
4.tip: Verses 10 to 12 can sound like a promise that wise living means no trouble, which may sting for someone who has suffered anyway. Name that honestly, and help the group read Proverbs as general patterns about how life works, not guarantees for every situation.

5.open: What is something that looked great in an ad or a photo but turned out to be a letdown when you got it?
questions: The writer says the lips of the forbidden woman "drip honey," but "in the end she is bitter as wormwood" (vv. 3, 4). Why is temptation so often sweet at the start and costly later?

The advice in verse 8 is "Keep your path far from her; do not go near the door of her house." Why not just tell someone to push through and say no at the last moment? What does keeping your distance look like in real life today, such as phones, work, friendships or late nights?

Verses 9 to 11 list what could be lost: strength, years, money and reputation. In Israel an affair could mean public disgrace before the whole community. What costs do you see today when trust is broken?
The man in verse 12 says, "How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!" Who in your life is allowed to tell you the truth, and what makes it hard or easy to listen?

Verses 15 to 19 turn warm and honest: "may you rejoice in the wife of your youth" (v. 18). What surprises you about the Bible speaking this openly about married love and desire? What does it suggest about how God sees them?
Verse 21 says "the LORD examines all his paths." Be honest: does that feel comforting, uncomfortable, or something else to you right now, and why?

Verse 22 says "the cords of his sin entangle him." Where have you seen small choices slowly become a trap? What would you want to say to someone who feels already tangled up, and who might be afraid it is too late?
5.life: Pick one small boundary this week that keeps you further from a temptation you know about, and tell one trusted person about it. If you are married, also do one specific kind thing for your spouse. If you are single, thank someone who has spoken honestly into your life.
5.prayer: Ask God for the wisdom to see where sweet things lead before you get there. Ask for honest friends, and for his mercy and help for anyone in the group who feels caught or hurt.
5.tip: This passage is written to a young man about adultery, and it may land hard for people who have been hurt by an affair or divorce. Say up front that no one has to share personal stories, and bring the discussion back to the wisdom and the grace in the text. Also name one point where Christians differ: most read the warning plainly as about adultery, but some have also read the woman as a picture of idolatry or false teaching. Mention it in one line and move on.

6.open: What is a small thing you keep putting off, even though you know it would be easier to just do it?
questions: A parent warns about a rash promise and says to "humble yourself" and get free quickly (v. 3). Why is it so hard to admit a mistake early? What would it look like to ask for help before things get worse?
The ant has no boss, yet it "prepares its provisions in summer" (v. 8). What is one ordinary habit you admire in someone else, and what could you learn from it?
Verse 10 says, "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest." How do you tell the difference between healthy rest and slowly drifting? What helps you notice?
The troublemaker is described as "winking his eyes, speaking with his feet, and pointing with his fingers" (v. 13). What are some quiet ways people stir up trouble today, in person or online?
The list of things the LORD hates ends with "one who stirs up discord among brothers" (v. 19). Why do you think God cares so much about how we treat one another? What does that show you about him?
Verse 23 calls wise teaching "a lamp" and "a light." Who has passed on wisdom to you, and how did it land? If you find it hard to trust that God's guidance is good, what makes it hard?

Verse 27 asks, "Can a man embrace fire and his clothes not be burned?" Where do we tell ourselves we can get close to something harmful without being hurt? And if someone already feels caught, verse 5 pictures escape "like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter." What might getting free look like, and who could help?
6.life: Pick one trap from this chapter that fits your life right now: a promise you rashly made, a task you keep delaying, or a habit you keep flirting with. Take one small, honest step this week, such as making a phone call, starting the task, or telling a trusted friend.
6.prayer: Ask God for the humility to admit mistakes early and the wisdom to see danger before it grows. Thank him that he is a God who rescues people who are stuck.
6.tip: Verses 24 to 35 are heavy, and someone in the room may carry shame or pain from an affair, either their own or someone else's. Don't dwell on the punishments. Keep the focus on the chapter's wider point, that small choices can lead to big harm, and remind the group that the call to "free yourself" (v. 5) is an invitation to come out of hiding and ask for help.

7.open: Have you ever walked or driven somewhere you knew you shouldn't go, just because it was on the way or you were curious? What happened?
questions: The father says to guard his teaching "as the apple of your eye" and to "write them on the tablet of your heart" (vv. 2, 3). What is something you protect that closely, and what would it take to treat wisdom that way?
In verse 4 the son is told to say to wisdom, "You are my sister." Why might the father use the language of family instead of rules? Who has been a wise voice that felt like family to you?

The young man is described as "lacking judgment" and is seen "strolling down the road to her house" at twilight (vv. 7, 8). Nobody forces him. What small steps in our own lives can slowly lead us toward places we would never choose on purpose?

The woman is "loud and defiant" and uses "flattering lips" (vv. 11, 21). Her words are warm and flattering, and she mentions a meal and a perfumed bed. Why do temptations so often sound like an invitation to something good?
She tells him, "my husband is not at home" (v. 19). What does her pitch assume about secrecy, and why does being unseen make wrong choices feel safer?

Verse 22 says he "follows her on impulse," and verse 23 says he does so "not knowing it will cost him his life." Where do you see people today not realizing the cost until it is too late? Where have you seen it in yourself?

Verse 25 says, "Do not let your heart turn aside to her ways." The warning is about the heart leaning, not just the final act. What would it look like to guard your heart early, long before the crisis?

This chapter is a stern warning, and some of us carry regret about past choices, or doubt that wisdom can reach us now. What would you want to say to someone who feels it is too late for them? What do you honestly hope is true about God's mercy?
7.life: Think of one place, habit or situation where you tend to drift toward trouble. This week, make one small change at the very start of that road, such as a different route, a boundary on your phone, or telling a trusted friend.
7.prayer: Ask God for the humility to hear wisdom before the crisis, and for a heart that leans toward him. Thank him that he is merciful to those who have already wandered.
7.tip: The chapter is aimed at young men, so women in the group may feel awkward or singled out, and the woman in the story can be read as a stereotype. Say plainly that the temptation is the point, not any group of people, and that everyone drifts. Christians also differ on whether this is mainly about adultery or about folly in a wider sense, so let both readings be heard. Keep the tone honest and gentle, since some in the room may carry real pain or shame about affairs.

8.open: Who is the person you call first when you have a decision to make, and what is it about them that you trust?
questions: Wisdom does not whisper from a quiet room. She takes her stand "at the crossroads" and "beside the gates to the city" (vv. 2-3). Why do you think the writer pictures wisdom calling out in the busiest places?
She calls to "O simple ones" and "O fools" (v. 5). What does it say about God that wisdom is offered to people who know they are lacking?
Wisdom says, "All the words of my mouth are righteous; none are crooked or perverse" (v. 8). When have you been given advice that sounded smart but turned out to be twisted?
Verse 10 says, "Receive my instruction instead of silver, and knowledge rather than pure gold." What do people around us tend to choose over wisdom, and what makes that choice so easy?
In verse 13 wisdom says, "To fear the LORD is to hate evil." What do you think it means to fear the LORD in a way that is not just being afraid?
Wisdom says, "I love those who love me, and those who seek me early shall find me" (v. 17). Where do you feel like you are still searching, or have not found much clarity? Be as honest as you like.

In verses 22 to 31 wisdom describes being there when God made the world, and being His "delight day by day" (v. 30). What picture of God comes through when wisdom is described as rejoicing in His presence and in people?

Verse 35 says, "whoever finds me finds life and obtains the favor of the LORD." Verse 34 pictures someone "watching daily at my doors" (v. 34). What would it look like for you to wait on wisdom like that in an ordinary week?
8.life: Pick one decision you are facing this week, big or small. Before you act, set aside ten minutes to pray about it and ask one person you trust for their honest view.
8.prayer: Thank God that wisdom calls out to everyone, including the simple and the unsure. Ask for a listening heart and the humility to take good advice.
8.tip: Verses 22 to 31 raise questions about whether wisdom was made or possessed, and whether this points to Christ. Name the disagreement in one line, since Christians read it differently, and bring people back to verses 1 to 21 and 32 to 36, where the call to listen is clear. Verses 18 to 21 can also sound like a promise of wealth, so gently ask the group what kind of riches wisdom might mean.

9.open: Think of a meal someone made for you that you still remember. What made it special?
questions: Wisdom "has built her house" and "set her table" before she invites anyone (vv. 1, 2). What does it say about wisdom that everything is ready before the guests arrive?
Her invitation is for "whoever is simple" (v. 4). Why do you think she calls the inexperienced and not the already clever? How does that sit with you?
She says, "Leave your folly behind, and you will live" (v. 6). What does it look like in everyday life to leave something behind in order to walk in a new way?
Verse 8 says, "rebuke a wise man, and he will love you." Think of a time someone corrected you. How did you respond, and what made it easier or harder to hear?
Verse 10 says "the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." What does respect and awe toward God mean to you, and is it easy or hard to feel right now? Be as honest as you like.
Folly sits "at the door of her house" and uses the very same words Wisdom used (v. 16). Why might the most harmful invitations sound a lot like good ones?
Folly says, "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is tasty!" (v. 17). Why can something feel more appealing when it is hidden or off limits?
Verse 18 says her guests do not know where they have ended up. What small choices can quietly lead people somewhere they never meant to go?
9.life: Pick one decision or habit this week where two voices are calling to you. Before you choose, stop and ask which table you are being invited to, and what the meal will cost you later. If you are brave, ask a trusted friend to speak honestly into it.
9.prayer: Ask God for ears that can hear correction without getting defensive. Pray for the humility to accept Wisdom's invitation and for the discernment to recognize Folly's.
9.tip: Verses 7 to 9 can sound like a label to stick on people, as if some are wise and some are mockers. Keep the focus on ourselves: ask how each of us responds when corrected. Also, Christians differ on whether Wisdom as a woman points to God's wisdom in general or to Christ himself. Say so in a sentence and move on, since the questions don't depend on it.

10.open: Who gave you a piece of advice when you were younger that you ignored at the time but later realized was right?
questions: Verse 1 says "A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish son grief to his mother." What do you think it meant for a family when this was written, and what does it say about how our choices affect the people who love us?
Verse 4 says "Idle hands make one poor, but diligent hands bring wealth." Verse 2 says "Ill-gotten treasures profit nothing." What do these two sayings together say about how God sees work and money?
Verse 9 says "He who walks in integrity walks securely." What does it look like to live the same way in private as in public, and where is that hardest for you?
Verse 12 says "Hatred stirs up dissension, but love covers all transgressions." Think of a time when someone chose not to expose or replay your mistake. What did that do for you?
Verse 19 says "When words are many, sin is unavoidable." Where do you find it hardest to hold your tongue: in conversation, in group chats, or online?
Verse 11 calls the mouth of the righteous "a fountain of life." Who in your life speaks that way, and what do they do that others do not?

Verse 3 says "The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry," yet many faithful people do struggle and suffer. Christians read sayings like this differently, some as promises and some as general patterns. How do you honestly hold that tension? It is fine to say you are unsure.
Verse 17 says "Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life." Who has the right to correct you, and how do you respond when they do?
10.life: Pick one habit from this chapter, either diligent work, honest dealing, or careful words, and practice it on purpose this week. At the end of each day, take a minute to notice how it went and ask God for help with tomorrow.
10.prayer: Ask God for a wise heart and for words that give life. Pray for anyone in the group who is struggling with work, money, or a broken relationship.
10.tip: Proverbs sayings can sound like guarantees, and someone who is jobless, sick, or grieving may hear them as blame. Say early that the group will treat these as wisdom about how life usually goes, not promises for every case, and let people share honestly where it has not worked out that way.

11.open: Think of a shop, a mechanic or a neighbor you would trust with almost anything. What made you trust them?
questions: Verse 1 says "Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, but an accurate weight is His delight." Why might God care about something as ordinary as a fair weight? What are the modern versions of rigged scales?
Verse 2 says "When pride comes, disgrace follows, but with humility comes wisdom." When have you seen pride trip someone up, or caught it tripping you?
Verse 3 says "The integrity of the upright guides them." How does being honest make decisions simpler, and when has it made them harder?
Verse 13 says "A gossip reveals a secret, but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence." Why is gossip so tempting, and what does it cost a community, such as a family, workplace or church?
Verse 15 warns against putting up security for a stranger. Does this mean we should never help someone in money trouble? How might you help wisely and still be generous?

Verse 25 says "A generous soul will prosper, and he who refreshes others will himself be refreshed." Where have you seen this happen? Where have you seen generous people left struggling, and how do you make sense of that?
Verse 28 says "He who trusts in his riches will fall." What do you find yourself leaning on for security, and what would it look like to lean more on God?
These sayings describe how life tends to go, but real life does not always match. Where does this chapter feel true to you, and where does it feel hard to believe? Be as honest as you like.
11.life: Pick one small area this week where you can be plainly fair or generous when nobody would notice, like giving an honest answer, paying what you owe, or quietly helping someone. Also pass on one piece of gossip by simply not repeating it.
11.prayer: Ask God for a heart that is honest in small things and open-handed with what you have. Pray for anyone in the group who feels that doing the right thing has cost them.
11.tip: Proverbs 11 can sound like a promise that good people always do well, and someone may be carrying a painful story that says otherwise. Present these as wisdom about how life usually tends to go, not a guarantee. Say plainly that Christians differ on whether the promises of rescue from death point mainly to this life or to judgment and reward after death. Let honest doubt be welcome, and do not rush to fix it.

12.open: Who is someone who always seems to know the right thing to say, and what is it about them?
questions: Verse 1 says "Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge." Most of us do not love correction. What makes it easier or harder for you to hear it from someone?
Verse 15 says "The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to counsel." Who do you actually listen to when you are making a decision, and why them?
Verse 18 says "Speaking rashly is like a piercing sword, but the tongue of the wise brings healing." Can you think of words someone said to you, good or bad, that stayed with you a long time?
Verse 16 says "a prudent man overlooks an insult." What is the difference between letting a slight go and pretending it did not hurt?
Verses 11 and 24 praise steady, ordinary work. How do you see work, as a burden, a calling, or something in between? Be honest.
Verse 25 says "Anxiety weighs down the heart of a man, but a good word cheers it up." What is weighing on you lately, and what kind of word would help?
Verse 21 says "No harm befalls the righteous." Many of us know good people who have suffered. How do you read a verse like this alongside real life? It is fine to say you are unsure.
Verse 22 says those who deal faithfully are "His delight." How does it land on you to hear that God delights in ordinary honesty and faithfulness?
12.life: Pick one person this week and give them a good word: a specific thank you or encouragement. Also ask one trusted person for honest feedback on something, and listen without defending yourself.
12.prayer: Ask God for a teachable heart and for words that heal instead of wound. Bring any worry that is weighing you down and ask for a good word from him.
12.tip: Verse 21 may stir up painful stories of good people who suffered. Do not rush to explain it. Say plainly that Christians differ on whether Proverbs gives general patterns or firm promises, let people share honestly, and point out that Job and other Scripture hold the tension too.

13.open: Who is someone you spent a lot of time with growing up, and what did you pick up from them without meaning to?
questions: Verse 1 says "a wise son heeds his father's discipline." Who has been a person in your life that you could take correction from, and what made it possible to listen?
Verse 3 says "He who guards his mouth protects his life." Think of a time when words came back around on you or someone you know. What happened?
Verse 7 describes people who pretend to be rich and others who pretend to be poor. Why do you think people put on a show about money? What does it cost them?
Verse 12 says "Hope deferred makes the heart sick." What does that look like in real life, and what has helped you, or someone you know, keep going while waiting?
Verse 20 says "He who walks with the wise will become wise." What would your friendships and habits say about who you are becoming? Where would you like that to change?

Verses 21 and 25 say the righteous prosper and the wicked go hungry. Christians differ on whether these are promises or general patterns, since good people sometimes suffer. How do you read them when life does not seem to work that way?
Verse 23 says "without justice" what the poor grow is "swept away." What does that suggest about how God sees poverty, and what might it ask of us?

Verse 24 speaks of a parent who "disciplines him diligently." Whatever you think about the method, what does the verse say about the link between love and correction? Where have you seen that done well, or badly?
13.life: Pick one habit from this chapter to work on this week: pausing before you speak, taking correction without defending yourself, or spending time with someone who is wiser than you. Notice what happens, and thank God for any small progress.
13.prayer: Ask God for a teachable heart and for words that build people up. Pray for anyone in the group who is waiting on something and feeling worn down by it.
13.tip: Verses 21 to 25 can sound like a guarantee that good people always do well, which can sting for someone who is struggling. Say plainly that Christians read these sayings differently, and that Proverbs describes how life usually goes, not a promise for every case. Leave room for people to say honestly that it has not worked that way for them.

14.open: What is a piece of advice from a parent or grandparent that you ignored at the time but later found was right?
questions: Verse 1 says "Every wise woman builds her house, but a foolish one tears it down with her own hands." What are some small everyday choices that build up a home or a friendship, and some that quietly tear it down?
Verse 4 says "Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty, but an abundant harvest comes through the strength of the ox." What do you think it means that good things come with some mess and effort?

Verse 10 says "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares in its joy." Verse 13 adds that "even in laughter the heart may ache." Who might be hurting behind a smile in your life, and how could you notice?

Verse 12 says "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death." Tell about a time something felt right and later looked different. How might a person check their road before they are far down it?

Verse 15 says "The simple man believes every word, but the prudent man watches his steps." What does it look like to be careful about what we hear and believe today without becoming suspicious of everyone?

Verse 20 says the poor man is hated even by his neighbor, while verse 21 says "blessed is he who shows kindness to the poor." Why do you think the chapter states the way things are and then points to a better way?
Verse 29 says "a patient man has great understanding," and verse 30 says "envy rots the bones." Which of these is harder for you right now, patience or contentment? What do you find helps?

Verse 26 says "He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence." If you are not sure what you believe about God, what would a safe place to stand look like for you? If you are, how has trusting God given you steadiness?
14.life: Pick one decision you are facing this week, big or small. Before you act, ask one wise person you trust to look at it with you, and listen to where they think the road leads.
14.prayer: Ask God for wisdom to build up the people around you with words and choices. Pray for anyone in the group who is carrying a hidden ache, and for patience where tempers run short.
14.tip: Proverbs gives general observations, not guarantees, so verses like 11 and 26 can sting people whose families or lives have fallen apart despite their best efforts. Say gently that these sayings describe how life tends to go, and that faithful people still suffer. Then steer back to the call to build wisely, with God's grace for the rest.

15.open: Think of a time someone said exactly the right thing at exactly the right moment. What did they say, and why did it help?
questions: Verse 1 says "A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger." Think of a time a calm reply cooled things down, or a sharp one made things worse. What happened?
Verse 4 calls a soothing tongue "a tree of life" and says a perverse tongue "crushes the spirit." Who has spoken words into your life that built you up, and what did they do for you?
Verse 28 says "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer." What would it look like for you to pause before answering, at home, at work or online?
Verse 3 says "The eyes of the LORD are in every place." Does that feel more comforting or more uncomfortable to you right now? Be as honest as you like.
Verse 5 says "whoever heeds correction is prudent," and verse 32 says ignoring discipline means despising yourself. Why is correction so hard to take, and who is safe enough in your life to give it?
Verse 17 says "Better a dish of vegetables where there is love than a fattened ox with hatred." What would a meal like that look like today, and what do we chase that costs us the love?
Verse 22 says "Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed." Where are you making a decision on your own that could use another voice?
Verse 33 says "humility comes before honor." What does humility look like in daily life, and how is it different from thinking badly of yourself?
15.life: Pick one conversation this week that might get tense. Before you answer, take one slow breath and aim for a gentle reply. Then ask one trusted person for honest feedback about something you are working on.
15.prayer: Ask God to guard your mouth and soften your heart. Pray for the humility to hear correction, and for words that bring life to the people around you this week.
15.tip: Verses like 6, 25 and 29 can sting for anyone who has been righteous and still struggled, or whose prayers feel unanswered. Say plainly that Christians differ on whether these are guaranteed promises or general patterns of how life usually works, and invite honest answers without trying to settle it.

16.open: Tell about a time you made a careful plan, like a trip, a meal or a project, and it went a different way than you expected.
questions: Verse 2 says "All a man's ways are pure in his own eyes, but his motives are weighed out by the LORD." Why is it so easy to believe our own motives are good? How might someone who loves us help us see more clearly?

Verse 3 says, "Commit your works to the LORD and your plans will be achieved." The word for commit means to roll a load onto someone stronger. What are you carrying right now that you could roll onto God?

Verse 9 says, "A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps." Christians differ on how much God's direction leaves room for human choice. Where do you land today, and what questions does it leave you with?

Verse 4 is a hard one, and readers take it in different ways. Some hear that wrongdoing meets a fitting end. Others hear that God can use even wicked people in his larger plans without making them wicked. What do you make of it, and what do you wish you could ask?
Verse 18 says, "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall." What does pride look like in everyday life, and how can you spot it in yourself?
Verse 24 says, "Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones." Think of a time someone's kind words helped you. What did they say, and why did it matter?

Verse 25 says, "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death." When have you been sure you were on the right path and later found you were not? What would you say to someone who feels unsure about which way to go right now?

Verse 32 says that someone who controls his temper is "greater than one who captures a city." Why might self-control be harder than winning something big? What helps you slow down when you feel angry?
16.life: Pick one plan or worry you are carrying this week and roll it onto God in prayer, as verse 3 describes. Then, once a day, say one kind and honest sentence to someone, remembering verse 24.
16.prayer: Ask God to show you your real motives and to help you hold your plans loosely. Thank him that he is steady when your plans change.
16.tip: Verses 4 and 9 can lead the group into a long debate about God's control and human freedom. Say once that Christians differ, let a couple of people share, then bring the group back to the chapter's practical call: humility, honest words and trusting God with our plans. Also leave room for anyone whose plans have fallen apart, and do not rush to tidy it up.

17.open: Think of a meal or gathering you remember for the right reasons. What made it good?
questions: Verse 1 says "Better a dry morsel in quietness than a house full of feasting with strife." When have you seen peace matter more than having plenty, in your home or anywhere else?
Verse 3 says the LORD is "the tester of hearts." What do you feel when you hear that God sees what is really in us: worry, relief, something else? Be as honest as you like.
Verse 5 says that whoever mocks the poor "insults their Maker." What does that tell us about how God sees people who have little? Where does that challenge how we talk or think?

Verse 9 says "Whoever conceals an offense promotes love, but he who brings it up separates friends." What does it look like to let a small wrong go? How is that different from pretending nothing happened?
Verse 14 says "To start a quarrel is to release a flood." Why do arguments grow so fast? What helps you step back before the flood breaks out?
Verse 17 says "A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity." Who has stayed beside you in a hard season, and what did that mean to you?
Verse 22 says "A joyful heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries up the bones." What does a heavy season feel like in your body? If you are in one now, what would help, even a little?
Verse 27 says "A man of knowledge restrains his words." When have you wished you had said less, and when did staying quiet cost you something?
17.life: This week, choose one small offense, a careless comment or a minor annoyance, and let it go without bringing it up again. Then reach out to one friend who may be going through a hard time and simply stay with them.
17.prayer: Ask God to give each person a calm spirit and careful words. Thank him for the friends who have stayed close, and pray for anyone in the group who feels worn down right now.
17.tip: Proverbs 17 is a string of separate sayings, so the group may jump around or struggle to find one theme. Let people pick the verse that stood out to them. Verses 2, 21 and 25 about foolish sons can sting parents who are hurting over a grown child, so say that proverbs describe general patterns and are not promises or verdicts on any one family.

18.open: Think of a friend who has stuck with you through something hard. What did they do that you still remember?
questions: Verse 2 says a fool delights "only in airing his opinions." When do you catch yourself waiting to talk instead of really listening?
Verse 8 says gossip goes down like "choice morsels" into "the inmost being." Why is gossip so tempting, and what does it do to the person who hears it?

Verse 10 says "The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe." What does it look like to run to God when you are scared or overwhelmed, and what do you tend to run to first?
Verse 11 says a rich man's wealth is "a high wall in his imagination." What do people trust for safety today that may not hold up in a real crisis?
Verse 13 says answering before you hear is "folly and disgrace." Can you share a time you jumped to a conclusion and got it wrong, or someone did that to you?
Verse 14 asks, "who can survive a broken spirit?" What helps a person who feels crushed inside, and what does not? If you are honestly running on empty yourself, you can say so here.
Verse 21 says, "Life and death are in the power of the tongue." Think of one thing someone said to you that gave you life, and one that did damage. What made the difference?
Verse 24 speaks of "a friend who stays closer than a brother." What makes a friend that dependable, and how can we be that for someone else?
18.life: This week, before you reply to someone in a tense or important conversation, pause and ask one more question to make sure you understand them first. Also say one encouraging word to someone who needs it.
18.prayer: Ask God to be your strong tower in whatever feels shaky right now. Ask for slower speech, listening ears, and words that build people up.
18.tip: Verse 22 about finding a wife can leave single, widowed or divorced people feeling left out. Acknowledge that gently, and point the group to the wider theme of the chapter: good relationships of every kind, including friendship in verse 24, are gifts from God.

19.open: Think of a time a plan of yours fell apart completely. What happened, and can you laugh about it now?
questions: Verse 1 says, "Better a poor man who walks with integrity than a fool whose lips are perverse." Why do you think the writer puts honesty above money? Where do you feel pressure to choose the other way?
Verse 3 says a person's "own folly subverts his way, yet his heart rages against the LORD." Why is it so easy to blame God or someone else when our own choices have gone wrong?

Verses 4 and 6 describe how people flock to the wealthy and the generous, while verse 7 says even relatives avoid the poor. These lines describe how people behave rather than approve of it. Where have you seen this happen, and how do you want to act differently?

Verse 11 says, "A man's insight gives him patience, and his virtue is to overlook an offense." Is there an offense you have been holding onto? What might it look like to let it go, or to deal with it kindly?
Verse 17 says, "Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender." What does this tell us about how God sees people in need? How could we respond this month?
Verse 20 says, "Listen to counsel and accept discipline, that you may be wise the rest of your days." Who speaks honestly into your life, and what makes it hard to hear correction from them?

Verse 21 says, "Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail." How does this land with you right now: as a comfort, a frustration, or something else? Be as honest as you like.
When something goes wrong in your life, how do you tell what came from your own choices and what was simply out of your hands?
19.life: Pick one saying from this chapter that stung a little, such as honesty, patience, taking advice or helping someone in need. This week, take one small, specific step on it, like owning a mistake you have been blaming on others, or giving practical help to someone who is struggling.
19.prayer: Thank God that his purpose stands even when our plans do not. Ask for honesty about our own choices, patience with people who irritate us, and open hands toward anyone in need.
19.tip: Verses 13 and 18 are the likely hard spots. Verse 13 is written from a husband's point of view and can sting, and verse 18 on disciplining a child is unclear in its second line, so it may warn about neglect or about punishing in rage. Don't try to settle the meaning. Say that proverbs are general observations rather than guarantees, note that the chapter also calls a sensible spouse a gift from the LORD (v. 14), and steer the group to verses where everyone can speak freely, such as honesty, patience and kindness to the poor.

20.open: Think of a time you bought something, or made a deal, and walked away feeling you had either won or been cheated. What happened?
questions: Verse 3 says, "It is honorable for a man to resolve a dispute, but any fool will quarrel." Why is walking away from a fight so hard to do, and what helps you do it?

Verse 5 says the intentions of the heart "are deep waters, but a man of understanding draws them out." Who in your life has helped you understand what was really going on inside you? What did they do?
Verse 6 asks, "who can find a trustworthy man?" What makes someone truly trustworthy, as opposed to someone who just says the right things?
Verse 9 asks who can claim to have kept their heart pure and to be cleansed from their own sin. How do you honestly answer that question, and what do you do with the answer?
Verses 10 and 23 say that differing weights and unequal measures are "detestable to the LORD." What are the modern versions of a crooked scale at work, in business or online?

Verse 17 says food gained by fraud "is sweet to a man, but later his mouth is full of gravel." Have you seen, in your own life or someone else's, a shortcut that tasted good at first and went bad later?
Verse 22 tells us not to take revenge, but to "Wait on the LORD, and He will save you." What makes waiting so difficult when you have been wronged? What might waiting look like in practice?

Verse 24 says, "A man's steps are from the LORD, so how can anyone understand his own way?" If you are in a season where you can't make sense of your path, or of God, what would you honestly say about it tonight?
20.life: Verse 27 calls the human spirit "the lamp of the LORD, searching out his inmost being." This week, take five quiet minutes each evening to ask what motive was really behind one thing you said or did that day. Tell God what you find, and rest in his grace rather than your own record.
20.prayer: Ask God to show you your own heart honestly and gently. Pray for the courage to deal fairly with others and for patience where you have been wronged.
20.tip: Verse 30 speaks of lashes and beatings cleansing evil, and verse 26 has a harsh threshing image. Some may hear these as approval of violence. Say plainly that these sayings reflect the culture and justice of their time, and that they are not a recipe for how we treat people. Then move on to the themes of honesty and the heart that fill most of the chapter.

21.open: What is a plan you made that looked great on paper but did not turn out the way you expected?
questions: Verse 2 says, "All a man's ways seem right to him, but the LORD weighs the heart." Can you think of a time you were sure you were right and later saw it differently? What changed your mind?

Verse 3 says that to do "righteousness and justice is more desirable to the LORD than sacrifice." What do you think that meant for people bringing offerings at the temple, and what might it mean for us when we worship or serve?
Verse 4 calls "haughty eyes and a proud heart" sin. Where does pride show up in ordinary life, and how can you spot it in yourself before others do?
Verse 13 warns that whoever "shuts his ears to the cry of the poor, he too shall cry out and receive no answer." Who is crying out near you, and what makes it easy to tune them out?

Verse 5 says the plans of the diligent "bring plenty," and verse 21 says whoever pursues righteousness and loving devotion "finds life, righteousness, and honor." Christians differ on whether these are firm promises or general patterns that often hold but not always. Where have you seen them hold true, and where have they seemed not to?
Verse 23 says, "He who guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from distress." When has something you said, or held back, made a real difference?

Verse 31 says, "A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD." What is the horse you tend to trust in, such as savings, skills, plans or connections? What is it like to let go of control, or to find that hard?
Verse 30 says no "wisdom, no understanding, no counsel" can prevail against the LORD. If you are honest, does that feel comforting, unsettling, or something else right now, and why?
21.life: Pick one decision you are facing this week, big or small. Before you act, ask yourself whether you are truly sure it is right or whether it just feels right. Then ask God to show you your real motives, and talk it over with one trusted person.
21.prayer: Ask God, who "weighs the heart" (v. 2), to show you your motives gently and without shame. Pray for help to be fair, honest and attentive to people in need, and to trust him with the outcomes you cannot control.
21.tip: Verse 9 and verse 19 speak about a quarrelsome wife and can sting or draw jokes. Name them as observations from a husband's view in an ancient household, not a verdict on women, and note that the point is how painful constant conflict is for anyone. Then steer the group back to the wider theme: God sees the heart.

22.open: Who is someone you would trust with your house keys, and what made you trust them?
questions: Verse 1 says "A good name is more desirable than great riches." Think of someone whose reputation you respect. What do you think earned it?
Verse 2 says "The LORD is Maker of them all," rich and poor alike. How would it change the way you treat people if you remembered that every day?
Verse 3 says "The prudent see danger and take cover." Can you think of a time you saw trouble coming and stepped aside, or a time you kept going and paid for it?

Verse 6 says "Train up a child in the way he should go." Proverbs usually describe what tends to happen, not what is guaranteed. Who helped shape you in a way that stuck? It is fine to answer with something that did not turn out the way people hoped.
Verse 9 says a generous person "shares his bread with the poor." When has someone's generosity reached you, and what did it do for you?
Verse 22 says "Do not rob a poor man because he is poor," and verse 23 says "the LORD will take up their case." Who today has little power to defend themselves, and what could we do about it?
Verse 25 warns that around an angry person "you may learn his ways." Whose habits are rubbing off on you right now, for better or worse?
22.life: Verse 2 says rich and poor share the same Maker. This week, give something quietly to someone in need, or sit down with someone you normally would not, and treat them as someone God made and loves.
22.prayer: Thank God that he is "Maker of them all." Ask him to help you see each person the way he does, and to make you someone whose good name is earned through kindness and fairness.
22.tip: Verse 6 can sting parents whose grown children have walked away. Say up front that this is a general pattern and not a promise, and that no one has to defend their family story. If verse 15 comes up, note that the rod reflects the discipline common in that culture, and keep the focus on the chapter's wider call to wisdom and fairness.

23.open: What is something you once wanted badly that turned out to be less satisfying than you expected?
questions: Verse 4 says, "Do not wear yourself out to get rich." What does it look like today to wear yourself out for money, and how can you tell when you are getting close to that?
Verse 5 says wealth "makes wings for itself and flies like an eagle to the sky." Have you seen money or security disappear faster than anyone expected? What did that teach you?
Verses 6 and 7 describe a host whose "heart is not with you." Why does a welcome feel so empty when it is not sincere, and how can we offer real hospitality?
Verses 10 and 11 warn against taking land from the fatherless, because "their Redeemer is strong." What does that tell us about how God sees people who have no one to speak up for them?

Verses 13 and 14 speak of striking a child with a rod. Christians differ on how to apply this today. What do you think the passage is trying to protect a child from, and what does good correction look like?

Verse 17 says, "Do not let your heart envy sinners." When have you looked at someone doing well by doing wrong and wondered if it was worth doing right? Be as honest as you like, including if you still wonder.
Verse 23 says, "Invest in truth and never sell it." What are some things people are tempted to trade truth for, and what has it cost you or someone you know?

Verses 29 to 35 paint a vivid picture of someone caught by drink. Why do you think the writer describes it in such detail, and how can we care for people who are caught in something like this without shaming them?
23.life: Pick one pull from this chapter that you know is real for you, such as money, food, drink or wanting approval. This week, tell one trusted person about it and ask them to check in with you.
23.prayer: Ask God for the wisdom to see traps before they close. Pray for anyone in the group or their families who is struggling with money, drink or a hard relationship, and ask for grace and a way forward.
23.tip: Verses 29 to 35 may land hard if someone in the room has lived with addiction, their own or a loved one's. Keep the tone kind rather than judging, don't ask anyone to share more than they want to, and remind the group that Proverbs gives wisdom and warning, not a verdict on any person.

24.open: What is a small chore or task you tend to put off, and what usually gets you moving on it?
questions: The chapter opens, "Do not envy wicked men or desire their company" (v. 1). When have you caught yourself envying someone who seemed to be getting ahead the wrong way?
Verse 3 says, "By wisdom a house is built and by understanding it is established." What do you think it means for a home or a family to be built on wisdom? What does that look like day to day?
Verse 6 says, "victory lies in a multitude of counselors." Who are the people you go to for advice, and what makes it hard to ask for help?

Verse 11 says, "Rescue those being led away to death." Verse 12 says pleading "we did not know about this" does not fool God. What are some situations today where it is easy to look away, and what might a small step toward helping look like?

Verse 16 says "a righteous man may fall seven times" and "still gets up." What does this say about what makes a person righteous? If you are in a season of falling, or doubting that you can get back up, what would help you most right now?
Verse 17 says, "Do not gloat when your enemy falls." When someone who wronged you has a setback, what do you notice happening inside you? Why is that hard to admit?

Verse 29 warns against saying you will do to someone just what they did to you. Many Christians read this alongside Jesus' teaching on loving enemies. What does it look like to let go of getting even?

The writer walks past a field where "thorns had grown up everywhere" (v. 31) and learns that "a little sleep, a little slumber" leads to need (vv. 33-34). Where in your life are small delays quietly adding up?
24.life: Pick one small thing you have been putting off, and do it this week. Then find one person whose advice you trust and ask them about something you have been handling alone.
24.prayer: Ask God for wisdom to build a home and a life that lasts. Pray for a heart free of envy and revenge, and for eyes to notice someone who needs help.
24.tip: Verses 17 and 18 can be confusing because the writer says God may "turn His wrath away" from the enemy. Scholars debate the exact sense, so do not get stuck there. Keep the group on the clear point: gloating over someone's fall is not the way of wisdom. Also, verse 16 can sound like a rule that good people always bounce back. Gently remind the group that it is a picture of hope, and make room for anyone who feels stuck.

25.open: Think of a time someone said exactly the right thing at exactly the right moment. What did they say, and what did it do for you?
questions: Verse 2 says, "It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out." What is something about God you wish you understood better, and how do you handle not knowing?

Verse 4 compares removing "the dross from the silver" to what happens when bad influences are taken away. What would it look like to clear something out of your own life so that something better could take shape?

Verse 8 warns against rushing to court, and verse 9 says to "argue your case with your neighbor without betraying another's confidence." Why is it so tempting to go public or bring in others when we are in a dispute? What might talking directly cost and gain?
Verse 11 says, "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver." Who in your life tends to say the right thing at the right time, and what do they do that makes it work?
Verse 12 speaks of "a wise man's rebuke to a listening ear." How do you usually respond when someone corrects you? What helps you actually listen?
Verses 16 and 17 say too much honey makes you sick and too many visits wear out a welcome. Where have you seen a good thing turn sour because there was too much of it?
Verse 20 says singing songs "to a heavy heart" is like vinegar on a wound. What has helped you, or someone you know, when sorrow was heavy? What did not help?
Verse 21 says, "If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat." Who is hard for you to be kind to right now? If you are not sure you can believe this verse yet, what makes it difficult?
25.life: Pick one conversation this week where you can slow down. Before you speak, ask yourself whether what you are about to say is true, kind and well timed. If you have a disagreement with someone, take one step to talk with that person directly and privately.
25.prayer: Ask God for words that fit the moment and for the self-control that verse 28 says we need. Pray for someone who is hurting, and for the grace to be kind to someone who is hard to love.
25.tip: Verses 21 and 22 can raise questions about the "burning coals" and whether kindness is meant to shame an enemy. Say plainly that scholars are not certain what the image means. Most read it as the sting of shame or a change of heart that kindness can stir. Then keep the group on the clear point, which is to feed the person who is hungry. Also be ready for verse 24, which is aimed at the men of its day, to draw a laugh or a wince. Name it lightly and move on to the larger theme of quarreling in any home.

26.open: What is the funniest excuse you have ever heard (or given) for getting out of something?
questions: The chapter opens with "snow in summer and rain at harvest" (v. 1). Why do you think the writer uses weather that is out of place to describe giving honor to a fool?

Verse 4 says "Do not answer a fool according to his folly," and verse 5 says "Answer a fool according to his folly." Why might both be true? Think of a time when staying quiet was wise and a time when speaking up was.

Verse 12 says, "There is more hope for a fool than for him" who is "wise in his own eyes." Why is it so hard to help someone who thinks they already have all the answers? Where do you catch that attitude in yourself?
The lazy person says, "A lion is in the road!" (v. 13). What are some modern versions of that excuse, and which ones do you tend to reach for?
Verse 17 compares meddling in a quarrel "not his own" to grabbing a dog by the ears. How do you tell the difference between helping a friend in conflict and meddling?
Verse 19 describes someone who hurts a neighbor and then says, "I was only joking!" When have words passed off as a joke actually stung? What helps a person tell the difference?
Verse 20 says, "Without wood, a fire goes out; without gossip, a conflict ceases." What does it look like in practice to be the person who stops adding wood?

The chapter ends with charming words over a hidden hatred (vv. 24-26). Maybe you have been hurt by someone like that, or you wonder whether your own words always match your heart. What comes up for you as you read it, and where do you need grace?
26.life: This week, pick one conversation where you would normally add wood to the fire, through gossip, a sharp comeback or a joke at someone's expense. Choose to stay quiet, change the subject or say something kind instead.
26.prayer: Ask God for the wisdom to know when to speak and when to stay silent. Ask him to make your words match your heart, and to forgive the times they have not.
26.tip: Verses 4 and 5 look like they contradict each other, and the group may want to settle it. Let them sit side by side, as the chapter does, and ask for real examples of each. Also be careful with the name-calling in this chapter: steer people toward their own habits rather than labeling someone in their life as a fool or a loafer.

27.open: Who is someone you would call if you had a flat tire at midnight, and what makes you trust them?
questions: Verse 1 says, "Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring." What plans do you tend to hold too tightly, and what would it look like to hold them more loosely?
Verse 2 says, "Let another praise you, and not your own mouth." Why do you think praise from someone else counts for more? When is it hardest for you not to promote yourself?
Verse 4 asks, "who can withstand jealousy?" and says it is worse than wrath or anger like a flood. Why might jealousy be harder to deal with than a sudden burst of temper?

Verse 6 says, "The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful." Think of a time someone told you something hard that turned out to be true. How did you take it then, and how do you see it now?
Verse 10 says, "better a neighbor nearby than a brother far away." Who has shown up for you in a hard time, and who could you show up for this week?
Verse 17 says, "As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another." Who sharpens you? What makes that kind of friendship work, and what would make you walk away from it?
Verse 21 says a man "is tested by the praise accorded him." Why would praise be a test? If you are honest, how do you tend to react when people speak well of you?

Verse 23 says, "Be sure to know the state of your flocks." What in your life is the equivalent of the flock, the ordinary things that keep your household going, and which one have you been neglecting? If you are not sure where you stand with God right now, you can say that here too.
27.life: Pick one friend this week and do one of two things: ask them to tell you honestly how you are doing, or offer a gentle, honest word they may need to hear. Do it kindly and listen without defending yourself.
27.prayer: Thank God for the people who have stayed close and spoken truth to you. Ask for humility to receive correction and for love that is honest instead of flattering.
27.tip: Verse 15 and 16 describe a quarrelsome wife from a husband's point of view, and it can land badly in a mixed group. Acknowledge it plainly as an ancient saying about constant quarreling in a home, note that Proverbs says similar things about quarrelsome people in general, and move on quickly to the friendship verses.

28.open: When you were a kid, what was something you tried to hide from a parent or teacher, and did it work?
questions: Verse 1 says "The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are as bold as a lion." Have you ever felt jumpy or on edge because of something you were hiding? What was that like?

Verse 13 says "He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy." Why do you think hiding is so tempting, and what does the promise of mercy change about it?

Verse 15 compares a wicked ruler to "a roaring lion or a charging bear" (v. 15). What do these sayings suggest about how leaders affect ordinary people, and how should that shape the way we think about those who lead us?

Verse 6 says "Better a poor man who walks with integrity than a rich man whose ways are perverse." Most of us feel the pull of money in some way. Where do you feel that pull, and what would integrity look like there?

Verse 9 says that if someone turns away from hearing God's teaching, "even his prayer is detestable." That sounds harsh. What do you think it is warning against, and how does it sit with what you know of God's grace?
Verse 26 says "He who trusts in himself is a fool." Where are you most tempted to rely only on your own judgment, and who helps you see what you might be missing?
Verse 23 says an honest rebuke earns more favor in the end than flattery. When has someone told you a hard truth in a loving way, and how did you respond?

Verse 27 says "Whoever gives to the poor will not be in need, but he who hides his eyes will receive many curses." Is there a need around you that it is easy to look away from? If you are not sure what you believe about all this, say so honestly.
28.life: Choose one thing you have been keeping hidden, a mistake, a debt, or an awkward truth. This week, bring it to God in plain words, and if it involves another person, take one small step toward making it right.
28.prayer: Thank God that those who confess and renounce their sins "will find mercy" (v. 13). Ask for the honesty to stop hiding and for open eyes toward people in need.
28.tip: Verses 9 and 17 can sound harsh, and verse 17 is unclear even to scholars. Don't get stuck on them. Say plainly that these are short sayings about patterns in life, not promises or verdicts on any one person, and steer back to verse 13, where honesty meets mercy.

29.open: Think of someone who told you something you didn't want to hear at the time, but you are glad now that you heard it. What did they say?
questions: Verse 1 warns about being "stiff-necked after much reproof." What does that stubbornness look like in everyday life, and whose correction is hardest for you to hear?

Verse 2 says "the people rejoice" when the righteous flourish and "the people groan" when the wicked rule. Where have you seen the character of a leader shape everyone under them, at work, at church or at home?
Verse 5 says a flatterer "spreads a net for his feet." How can you tell the difference between real encouragement and flattery, in what you give and in what you receive?
Verse 11 says "a wise man holds it back" when it comes to anger. What helps you pause before you react, and what makes that hard for you?

Verse 7 says the righteous "consider the cause of the poor," and verse 13 says "the LORD gives light to the eyes of both" the poor and the oppressor. What does this tell us about how God sees people, and how might that change the way we treat them?

Verse 18 says "the people cast off restraint" where there is no vision, which here means a word from God. What happens to you when you go a long time without listening for God? Where does that feel true right now?
Verse 25 says "the fear of man is a snare." Whose opinion has the most pull on you? And if trusting the LORD feels hard or distant for you at the moment, what makes it hard?
29.life: This week, ask one person you trust whether there is something you are not hearing. Listen without defending yourself, then thank them and bring what you heard to God.
29.prayer: Ask God for a soft heart that can take correction without getting defensive. Pray for the leaders in your community, and for courage to trust God more than the opinions of other people.
29.tip: Verses 15, 17, 19 and 21 speak of the rod and of household servants, and they can stir strong feelings. Say that these sayings come from an ancient household, that Christians differ on how to apply the rod verses today, and then steer the group back to the larger themes of listening, fairness and humility.

30.open: What is something you have more than enough of at home, and something you never seem to have enough of?
questions: Agur begins, "I am weary, O God, and worn out" (v. 1), and then says he has not learned wisdom (v. 3). What do you make of a wise saying that starts with an admission like that?
In verse 4 Agur asks, "Who has gathered the wind in His hands?" Which part of the world, or of your own life, reminds you that you are not in control?
Verse 5 says, "Every word of God is flawless; He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him." When has something you read or heard from God felt like shelter, and when has it felt hard to trust?
Agur prays, "Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion" (v. 8). What would "enough" look like for you, and how would you know when you had it?
In verse 9 Agur fears that having too much might lead him to ask, "Who is the LORD?" and that having too little might lead him to steal. Which danger feels closer to you right now, and why?
Verses 15 and 16 describe things that "never say, 'Enough!'" Where do you see that endless wanting in our culture, and where do you see it in yourself?
Verses 24 to 28 praise small creatures that are "exceedingly wise" without much strength, like ants that "store up their food in the summer" (v. 25). What can we learn from being small but wise?
Verse 32 says that if you have exalted yourself or plotted evil, "put your hand over your mouth." Think of a time when stopping before you spoke would have saved you trouble. What happened?
30.life: Agur asked for enough, not more. This week, pick one area where you tend to want more, such as money, time, attention or stuff. Each time the wanting shows up, pause and thank God for one thing you already have.
30.prayer: Ask God to give you what you need and to keep you from both pride and panic. Pray for honesty with him about where you feel weary, as Agur was.
30.tip: Verse 4 asks about God's son, and Christians read it differently. Some take it as poetry about God's greatness, and others see a hint of Jesus. Say that in one line, then move on. Also, verses 22 and 23 reflect the social order of their time and can sound harsh, so treat them as ancient observation, not as advice for how to treat people today.

31.open: Who is someone you know who works hard and rarely gets thanked for it?
questions: The chapter begins with "the words of King Lemuel" that "his mother taught him" (v. 1). Who taught you something that has stayed with you, and what was it?
His mother warns him about drink because it could lead rulers to forget "what is decreed, depriving all the oppressed of justice" (v. 5). What does she seem to be most worried about for him?
Verses 6 and 7 say strong drink is for "one who is perishing" so he can "forget his poverty." Some readers hear compassion here and others hear a contrast with the king. How do you read it?
She tells him, "Open your mouth for those with no voice" (v. 8). Who has no voice in your town, workplace or school, and what could speaking up look like for you?
The poem asks, "A wife of noble character, who can find?" (v. 10). The Hebrew suggests strength and capability. How does that change the way you hear the word "noble"?

She "works with eager hands," buys a field and plants a vineyard (vv. 13, 16), and she also "opens her arms to the poor" (v. 20). What stands out to you about how her work and her generosity fit together?
Verse 25 says she "can laugh at the days to come." What makes it hard to face the future without fear, and what helps you?
Verse 30 says "Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised." Honestly, does this poem feel like encouragement or pressure to you right now? Why?
31.life: Pick one person who works quietly for others and thank them this week, in person or in writing, by naming something specific they do. If you want to go further, ask yourself where you could speak up for someone who has no voice.
31.prayer: Thank God for the people who taught you and the people who carry others quietly. Ask for a heart that fears the LORD more than it chases approval, and for courage to speak up for someone who needs it.
31.tip: Verses 10 to 31 can leave some people feeling they fall short, and Christians read the poem differently: as a model for wives, as strength open to anyone, or as a picture of Wisdom herself. Say that plainly, then steer the group toward the qualities the poem praises, like strength, generosity, wisdom and reverence for God, rather than a checklist of tasks. Make sure men, singles and anyone who feels overwhelmed know the poem speaks to them too.
